title: The needs for HIV treatment and care of children, adolescents, pregnant women and older people in low-income and middle-income countries
The position statement of the Working Group of the Polish Psychiatric Association on the use of D2/D3 dopamine receptor partial agonists in special populations.
abstract: D2/D3 dopamine receptor partial agonists (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine) are increasingly often used in the treatment of mental disorders due to a more favourable tolerability profile as compared to other antipsychotics. The article presents the position statement on the use of these drugs in the treatment of special populations: people with comorbid somatic diseases, people over 65 years of age, including those with dementia, children and adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women. The position statement was developed by the panel of experts appointedby the Executive Board of the Polish Psychiatric Association consisting of people experienced in the treatment of patients with mental disorders. The evaluation included the analysis of literature databases and information obtained from summaries of product characteristics, as well as reports and registers on the safety of the three evaluated drugs. D2/D3 dopamine receptor partial agonists can be used in the treatment of people who must be provided with the highest safety standards of the therapy. It results from their low risk of producing side effects, such as weight gain, metabolic disorders, akathisia, extrapyramidal symptoms, increased prolactin levels, prolongation of QTinterval in ECG, sedation and anticholinergic effects. Since dopamine receptor partial agonists are available for arelatively short time, there is less information on their use in pregnant women than for other antipsychotics.

title: Special issue on Women and HIV to mark International Women’s Day
abstract: International Women's Day is marked annually on 8 March and is a global day to celebrate the achievements of women, to raise awareness about equality for women and to lobby for accelerated gender parity. This year's campaign theme (#BreakTheBias) encourages us all to imagine a world that is free of bias and discrimination, a world that is diverse, equitable and inclusive and a world where difference is valued and celebrated. Notwithstanding unprecedented (preCOVID) advances in our knowledge about HIV, and dramatic improvements in both the diagnosis and treatment of HIV over a period of 30 years, which changed our perception of HIV from a terminal disease to a condition with normal life expectancy, gender inequality remains a major problem. This is despite the fact that globally over half of all people living with HIV are women. It has long been known that there are direct and indirect genderspecific determinants which can modulate viral recognition and immune activation, due to an interplay of genetics, sex hormones and environmental factors. As a result, women can present with lower HIV viral load levels than men in primary infection, but develop an AIDSdefining illness more rapidly, even after the same duration of infection. Regardless of this knowledge, the evidence to support the best treatment for women living with HIV remains suboptimal, with women continuing to be underrepresented in HIV studies; this results in many critical knowledge gaps. There is a historic rationale for this underrecruitment of women to clinical research studies: in the 1960s, unregulated and untrialled nonHIV drugs were given to pregnant women, resulting in foetal death and congenital abnormalities. As a result, those wishing to conduct drug research involving women have to navigate huge barriers and incur high costs to complete this research. This has resulted in an underrecruitment of women to drug trials in many clinical areas, including cardiac and renal medicine. Within the HIV setting, a recent review of randomized controlled trials showed that HIV pharmaceutical trials comprised only 7% black women but 50% white men; this is in contrast to the global HIV population of which black women make up 42% but white men only 6% [1]. It is clear that women must be seen as individuals who deserve the best care for their own health, and not simply as ‘potential pregnancies’. To support International Women's Day, HIV Medicine is excited to publish this special issue on the topic ‘Women and HIV’, the key aim of which is to highlight original highquality research that is being undertaken to support the clinical care and management of women living with HIV. The papers cover a wide range of topics, including the optimal clinical management of women with HIV (see papers by Hully et al. and Odongpiny et al.), service and care provision for transgender women (LacombeDuncan et al.), the screening for and management of comorbidities in women with HIV (Raffe et al., Campbell et al., Ashraf et al.), screening and management of human papillomavirus infection in women (Gupta et al., Cicconi et al.), issues around pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes (Rasi et al., Venkatesh et al.), as well as ageing and menopause (Hachfeld et al., Chirwa et al., Tariq et al.). Finally, Courvoisier et al. describe the barriers to participation in clinical research for women living with HIV. While we cannot hope to rectify a longstanding inequality with a single issue of the journal, the findings from the papers included contribute to building the research evidence that will support women living with HIV to age healthily and maintain the best possible quality of life. We look forward to a more equitable future where a special issue on this topic is no longer required.
